claims.claim: Clinical ethics concerns the right course of action for an individual patient's care, whereas organizational or administrative ethics concerns the right conduct of the institution and its managers in policy, finance, and operations; a substantial share of hospital ethics programs now address organizational and business ethics in addition to clinical ethics.

Tom Beauchamp and James Childress articulated four principles of biomedical ethics, respect for autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice, in their book Principles of Biomedical Ethics, first published in 1979; they are prima facie principles to be balanced through judgment rather than absolute rules.

Each of the four principles has a recognized meaning: respect for autonomy honors a person's capacity for informed self-determination; beneficence is acting for the person's benefit; non-maleficence is avoiding harm (the traditional 'first, do no harm'); and justice is the fair distribution of benefits, risks, and costs.

The ACHE Code of Ethics sets standards of conduct for healthcare executives in their relationships with colleagues, patients or others served, their organization, the community, and society; it directs executives to prioritize patient care and, where resources are limited, to ensure a resource-allocation process reflecting fairness, equity, and transparency.

The ACHE Code of Ethics addresses conflicts of interest by directing executives to disclose and, when required after board review, avoid financial and other conflicts of interest, and to implement an organizational code of ethics including conflict-of-interest principles and whistleblower protections and ensure competent ethics resources are available for staff.

A 2021 national survey estimated that about 97 percent of US hospitals maintain a health care ethics program; nearly all provide clinical ethics functions, while smaller shares also address ethical leadership, regulatory compliance, business ethics, and research ethics, and programs commonly provide ethics consultation, policy work, and education.

The Belmont Report, published April 18, 1979 by the National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral Research, identifies three basic ethical principles for research involving human subjects: respect for persons, beneficence, and justice.

In the Belmont Report, respect for persons incorporates two convictions, that individuals be treated as autonomous agents and that persons with diminished autonomy are entitled to protection; beneficence is treated as an obligation with two rules, do not harm and maximize possible benefits while minimizing possible harms; and justice concerns fairness in the distribution of the benefits and burdens of research.

An administrator holds a fiduciary duty to act in the interest of patients, the organization, and the public rather than for personal gain, which makes stewardship of finite resources an ethical obligation and puts stewardship in permanent tension with access; the ethical response is a fair, transparent allocation process rather than a formula.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether organizational ethics is a subcategory of clinical ethics, a form of business ethics, or a distinct domain, and whether existing clinical ethics committees should take it on.
positions: For decades US healthcare institutions focused ethics committees primarily on clinical rather than organizational questions.

A 2021 national survey shows many hospital ethics programs now also address organizational, leadership, and business ethics, and there are calls for integrated programs spanning clinical, organizational, and research ethics.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents clinical and organizational ethics as distinct altitudes of the same field, notes that ethics committees increasingly address both, and does not claim the boundary is settled.

sourceRecords.title: The Belmont Report: Ethical Principles and Guidelines for the Protection of Human Subjects of Research
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office for Human Research Protections (National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral Research)
sourceRecords.notes: US government work, public domain. Read the full report text via an Internet Archive id_ capture of the canonical HHS OHRP page (direct hhs.gov fetch returned Access Denied). Supports: the report's date (April 18, 1979) and issuing body; the three basic ethical principles for research with human subjects (respect for persons, beneficence, justice); that respect for persons incorporates treating individuals as autonomous agents and protecting those with diminished autonomy; that beneficence carries two rules (do no harm; maximize benefits and minimize harms); and that justice concerns fairness in distribution of research burdens and benefits. Canonical HHS URL registered; archive copy is the one actually read.

sourceRecords.title: The Four Principles (Ethical Frameworks)
sourceRecords.notes: Clinical-ethics network reference page. Confirms the four-principles approach is credited to Beauchamp and Childress in their book Principles of Biomedical Ethics, first published in 1979; names and defines the four principles (respect for autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice); and describes them as prima facie principles balanced through judgment (reflective equilibrium) rather than absolute rules. Used for attribution and standard definitions; no prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: ACHE Code of Ethics
sourceRecords.notes: Copyrighted professional code (as amended by the ACHE Board of Governors Dec. 8, 2025). Read in full via curl with a browser user-agent. Supports: the code's purpose as a standard of conduct for healthcare executives; its coverage of relationships with the profession, patients or others served, the organization, employees, and the community and society; the directive to prioritize patient care and to ensure, where resources are limited, a resource-allocation process reflecting fairness, equity, and transparency; and the conflict-of-interest provisions (disclose and, when required after board review, avoid financial and other conflicts of interest; implement an organizational code of ethics with conflict-of-interest principles and whistleblower protections; ensure competent ethics resources for staff). Described in original wording; no code text reproduced.
